faults.fault: a number with the wrong kind or source
faults.finding: 50 Hz is listed as a constant from source 4, whose quote gives only the 230 V nominal and its limits. It is used only in ignores.
faults.fix: Say 'at mains frequency' in ignores and drop the 50 Hz number.

faults.fault: a footnote on reasoning the quote lacks
faults.finding: 'about 0.707 of the peak, the peak ÷ √2.[^2]' puts source 2's footnote on the ÷ √2 step, which its quote does not state.
faults.fix: Footnote the 0.707 alone, then a separate sentence: that is 1 ÷ √2, as 70.7 V from a 100 V peak shows.

faults.fault: a footnote on a claim its quote does not make
faults.finding: 'Those figures are rms' follows the ENA footnote, whose quote does not say rms; the WJEC quote says 230 V is RMS.
faults.fix: 'The 230 V is an rms figure, so the wave peaks at about 230 × √2 = 325 V.[^3]'

faults.fault: false absolute / claim that fails after a later idea
faults.finding: 'Work heat and power with rms values just as you would with DC, P = V² ÷ R' is true for a resistance but not for a motor or any coil or capacitor, which lessons 4, 5 and 8 cover; read alone in the dossier it would mislead.
faults.fix: Limit it to a resistance and say coils and capacitors need more, in later lessons.

faults.finding: 'The peak is always the bigger figure' fails for a square wave, whose rms equals its peak; 'a square wave sits at its peak almost the whole time' blurs that it sits at the peak one way and then the other.
faults.fix: 'For a sine the peak is the bigger figure'; 'sits at its full height, one way or the other, almost the whole time'.

faults.fault: a general claim wider than its case
faults.finding: 'Read a voltage or current on a label ... as rms' would also cover DC equipment.
'what a square wave of 100 V peak really is in rms terms when such a meter shows 111 V' is hard to parse.
faults.fix: 'Such a meter shows 111 V on a square wave whose peak is 100 V. What is its rms value?'

shape.rule in words: yes: the steady DC giving the same heat
shape.worked example with real numbers: yes: 10 Ω, 100 V peak, 1000 W top, 500 W average, 70.7 V; and the 1 kW heater in practice
shape.misconception shown failing: yes: the average 63.7 V heats only 406 W; 163 V as the wrong-way conversion; 0.707 on a triangle
shape.analogy from his trade with where it bre: yes: a cable on an on-off load, 5 A average but 10 A heat-equivalent; breaks on slow cycles and on shape
shape.put it into practice: steps, rule of thumb, worked example, mistakes, safe way first

verdict: rewrite as draft 2 with the seven fixes
